original.target_description: Study 3 first scenario experiment: 80 Cornell undergraduates judge who feels more regret immediately on learning a transfer/stay decision was mistaken; short-term action-versus-inaction binomial comparison. This measures hypothetical regret intuitions, rather than participants’ own recent regrets.

n.sample_role: Cornell undergraduate respondents in the within-subject scenario experiment; each answered the initial and long-run questions.
n.exclusions: No exclusions or missing responses reported; the procedure explicitly assigns both questions to each subject.
n.location: p. 360 (source p. 4), Studies 3 and 4, first scenario procedure

notes: Identity checked independently: supplied text gives The Temporal Pattern to the Experience of Regret, Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Husted Medvec, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1994, Vol. 67, No. 3, 357–365. Title/authors/year/volume/pages match the neutral original reference. The DOI is not printed in the supplied text and was not independently resolved. This is an original empirical journal article, not the 2022 replication or a preregistration. Text spans pp. 357–365 but contains an incomplete Study 4 statistical line; no PDF was supplied for layout verification. Canonical text remains the evidence source. Only assigned unfinished fields are populated; other fields are unassigned placeholders. Study 3 is identified by the first scenario experiment under the joint Studies 3 and 4 heading, not by row order or statistic matching. The description’s recent-regret wording is operationalised here as the immediate/short-term hypothetical regret judgment, as anchored by study 3 and p. 4. The separate long-run candidate is binomial z = 2.35, p < .02 and is not pooled with the initial-regret test.
